questions.prompt: Explain the validate-before-mutate rule as BorrowBox applies it to reservations and checkouts: what is the required order of steps, and what went wrong before the repair?

keyPoints.text: Read all references, capture the time once, construct the candidate, check every precondition.
keyPoints.quote: Read all references, capture the operation time once, construct the candidate domain object, and check all state preconditions.

keyPoints.text: Only after that mutate the live equipment and persist the related record.
keyPoints.quote: Only then mutate the live equipment and persist the related record.

keyPoints.text: A failed candidate construction must leave the live object in its original state.
keyPoints.quote: If candidate construction fails, a live object must still have its original state.

keyPoints.text: The original reservation bug: the constructor threw after the equipment had already become Reserved.
keyPoints.quote: An expiry before the current time makes the constructor throw after `equipment.Status` has become Reserved.

keyPoints.text: The checkout twin: TryCheckOutAsync ran before new Loan, so a bad due date left the item CheckedOut.
keyPoints.quote: a bad due date used to run `TryCheckOutAsync` before `new Loan`, leaving equipment CheckedOut.

questions.prompt: Why does BorrowBox treat time as an input, and which equality rules hold at each time boundary (reservation creation, expiry processing, returns)?

keyPoints.text: Mixing UtcNow in one service with an injected clock in another makes boundaries inconsistent in tests.
keyPoints.quote: Using `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow` in one service and an injected clock in another means tests can observe inconsistent boundaries.

keyPoints.text: Capturing a single instant per operation removes a clock tick between validation and construction.
keyPoints.quote: One captured instant per operation prevents a clock tick between validation and construction.

keyPoints.text: Creating a reservation needs a strictly future expiry so an already-due item never becomes Active.
keyPoints.quote: Reservation creation requires a strict future expiry because an item that is already due should never enter Active state.

keyPoints.text: The expiry run is inclusive: a deadline of exactly now counts as due.
keyPoints.quote: Expiry processing uses an inclusive comparison because a reservation whose deadline is exactly now is due.

keyPoints.text: A return may happen at the checkout instant but never before it.
keyPoints.quote: Return timestamps are instants and may equal checkout, but never precede it.

questions.prompt: What does the in-memory lock, and later a database transaction, actually buy you, and what does neither of them protect against?

keyPoints.text: The per-item lock gives one winner when two checkouts target the same item.
keyPoints.quote: `TryCheckOutAsync` uses a lock on the equipment item, so two checkout attempts for one item still have one winner.

keyPoints.text: It does not protect the borrower loan-limit check when the items differ.
keyPoints.quote: That lock does not protect borrower-limit checks across distinct equipment.

keyPoints.text: Stores return live references, so comparing the same reference before and after is blind to mutation.
keyPoints.quote: A test that compares the same reference before and after cannot detect mutation.

keyPoints.text: Ordering limits damage from rejected operations but is not durable atomicity.
keyPoints.quote: Validation ordering reduces rejected-operation damage but is not durable atomicity.

keyPoints.text: A transaction makes writes atomic but cannot make a throwing constructor harmless.
keyPoints.quote: A transaction makes writes atomic; it does not make a constructor that throws harmless.

keyPoints.text: Isolation levels, unique indexes and RowVersion guard against concurrency, never against a well-formed request that should have been refused.
keyPoints.quote: they never protect you from a well-formed request that should have been refused.
